claims.claim: Drama is a literary form written to be performed; a play reaches full expression when watched and heard in performance, and reading the script is a different experience.
A play script is built from dialogue and stage directions; stage directions indicate who is on stage and what characters are aware of, and they are part of the printed play text.
Play texts organize their action into units such as acts and scenes, which modern editions mark clearly for readers.
Basic dramatic structure names the exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, and resolution (denouement), a common order rather than an invariant formula.

Tragedy and comedy are broad dramatic modes: tragedy typically moves toward suffering and aims to arouse pity and fear, while comedy involves humorous or lighter events; the categories reach back to Greek drama and Aristotle's Poetics.
Aristotle describes the tragic hero as a person of note whose misfortune comes not from vice and depravity but from some error of judgment (hamartia), an error rather than a moral failing.
A soliloquy is a speech by a character alone on stage that reveals the character's innermost thoughts directly to the audience.
An aside is a brief remark spoken while other characters are on stage that those characters are not supposed to hear and that is intended for the audience alone.
A monologue is an extended speech delivered by a single character, which may be addressed to others on stage or to the audience; a soliloquy is one kind of monologue.
Dramatic irony is an effect in which the audience knows more than a character does; it is felt in the gap between the audience's knowledge and the character's understanding during performance.
Every performance of a play is a unique live event: the script is stable, but actors' choices, staging, timing, and the audience make no two performances identical.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Soliloquy and aside are sometimes treated as the same convention.
positions: Pima Open's literary-terms list defines soliloquy as 'the actor is speaking to himself, or aside as it also is called', treating aside as a synonym for soliloquy.

LibreTexts Theater Appreciation defines the soliloquy as a monologue in which a single character shares innermost thoughts directly with the audience, and Dictionary.com defines an aside as lines supposedly not heard by others on stage and intended only for the audience.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson defines the two speech roles separately, uses Dictionary.com for the aside definition, and notes explicitly that some reference works blur the terms. Pima is cited for dialogue and soliloquy's general use, never for the aside definition.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Genre labels as strict categories versus broad modes.
positions: LibreTexts Theater Appreciation notes that a production can be assigned a genre by script content or by cultural movement, and that a production is rarely just one genre.
Textbook treatments commonly present tragedy and comedy as the two foundational dramatic forms.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents tragedy and comedy as broad dramatic modes with a long history, and avoids implying that every play belongs cleanly to exactly one genre.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Wording of the tragic hero's failing: 'tragic flaw' versus 'error of judgment'.
positions: LibreTexts Theater Appreciation renders Aristotle's concept as a 'tragic flaw', a mistake in judgment caused by a lack of knowledge.
Aristotle's Poetics (Bywater translation) says the misfortune is brought upon the hero 'not by vice and depravity but by some error of judgement'.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses hamartia as error of judgment, matching the primary text, and explicitly distinguishes the error from a moral character flaw.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft's boilerplate claim that drama is 'a foundational concept' students use to organize information was generic and unsupported; replaced with verified content.
The draft's vocabulary entries (context, evidence, application) were generic learning-meta terms, not drama terms, and were discarded.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the machine-generated boilerplate lesson with a source-verified lesson on drama as a performed literary form.
Defined soliloquy and aside as distinct speech roles rather than synonyms, correcting the conflation found in pima-literary-terms.
Named dramatic irony only as a performance-audience effect and left the in-depth treatment to the sibling irony topic.
rightsIssues: No blocking issues. All OER, university writing-lab, and dictionary sources were used reference-only with facts synthesized in original prose.
Aristotle's Poetics (Bywater translation, Project Gutenberg) is public domain; only a few words are quoted.
One brief line from Shakespeare's Hamlet ('To be, or not to be', Act 3, Scene 1) is quoted with attribution; the play is in the public domain.

sourceRecords.title: Reading a Play (Writing in Literature: Detailed Discussion)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21. Supports: it helps immensely to see a play performed; stage directions should not be skipped because knowing who is on stage reveals what characters are aware of; when one character is alone on stage the reader usually gets that character's thoughts and motivations; before the 20th century audiences said they had 'heard' a play; a play happens in real time and in the ear; reading scenes aloud lets the hidden drama of a printed play out into its natural element.

sourceRecords.title: Theater Appreciation (Lumen): 1: Introduction to Theater
sourceRecords.notes: Read the chapter subpage (1.01 Part One: Creating a World, Chapter 1 Mapping Reality) on 2026-08-21. Supports: Western theatrical practice traced to fifth-century BCE Athens, beginning with dithyrambs honoring Dionysus and becoming Greek tragedy presented at festivals; Aristotle's Poetics as the early account of drama; every performance is singular, no two are the same; soliloquy as a monologue in which a single character shares innermost thoughts as a direct appeal to the audience; the Oedipus discussion naming exposition, climax, falling action, and denouement (denouement meaning untying or unraveling, when final loose ends are resolved).

sourceRecords.title: Theater Appreciation (Lumen): 2: Genre
sourceRecords.notes: Read the chapter subpage (2.01 Part Three: Special Topics, Chapter 7 Genre) on 2026-08-21. Supports: Aristotle's Poetics (c. 335-323 BCE) as a work defining ancient Greece's two most prevalent dramatic forms, tragedy and comedy; genre assigned by script content (funny events = comedy, tragic events = tragedy) or by cultural movement; a production is rarely just one genre; Aristotle's view that tragedy features an important, heroic character with a 'tragic flaw', a mistake in judgment caused by a lack of knowledge, and aims to instill pity and fear leading to catharsis.

sourceRecords.title: Theater Appreciation (Lumen): 5: The World of Shakespeare
sourceRecords.notes: Read the chapter subpage (5.01 Part Three: Special Topics, Chapter 8 The World of Shakespeare) on 2026-08-21. Supports: readers of Shakespeare's printed texts encounter more than spoken words, including punctuation, spelling, typography, and stage directions; modern editions offset stage directions and mark clear breaks between scenes, unlike early modern printed texts; stage directions are part of the printed play text.

sourceRecords.title: The Poetics of Aristotle (Project Gutenberg ebook 6763, Ingram Bywater translation)
sourceRecords.notes: Read the Gutenberg HTML edition (6763-h) on 2026-08-21. Chapter XIII supports: the tragic hero is a person not pre-eminently virtuous and just, whose misfortune is brought upon him not by vice and depravity but by some error of judgement; the change in fortune runs from happiness to misery; tragedy arouses pity and fear. The lesson quotes only the short phrase 'error of judgement' in paraphrase context and attributes the account to Aristotle.
